hero.title: Diamond Bow Tie Effect: What It Is and When It Becomes a Problem
hero.subheading: Learn why oval, pear and marquise diamonds show a central bow-tie pattern, how to judge its darkness and movement, and when the effect should stop a purchase.

paragraphs: A bow-tie effect is a dark pattern that appears across the centre of certain elongated diamonds. It is most commonly associated with oval, pear and marquise diamonds, although related contrast patterns can appear in some heart, radiant and elongated cushion diamonds.
The pattern receives its name because its two darker sections can resemble the shape of a bow tie.

A visible bow tie does not automatically mean that a diamond is poorly cut. Contrast is necessary for a diamond’s facet pattern to look defined and lively. A subtle bow tie may add character and disappear into a balanced pattern as the diamond moves.

The concern begins when the bow tie is excessively dark, wide, uneven or persistent. A strong bow tie can divide the diamond visually and make the centre appear lifeless even while the ends remain bright.
Because the strength of a bow tie is not adequately communicated by carat, colour, clarity, polish or symmetry grades, the actual diamond must be inspected.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer
quickAnswer.question: A diamond bow tie is acceptable when it:
attributes: Appears light grey rather than black
Covers only a limited central area
Blends into the surrounding facet pattern
Does not dominate the face-up appearance
Remains unobtrusive at a normal viewing distance
closingParagraphs: A bow tie becomes a concern when it:
closingBullets: Forms a wide band across the complete centre
Is visible under several types of lighting
Divides the diamond into two bright ends
Appears more noticeable than the diamond’s sparkle
Creates an uneven or distracting central pattern
finalParagraphs: There is no official universal percentage or table-and-depth combination that can guarantee a minimal bow tie. The actual diamond must be viewed face-up, in motion and under realistic lighting.

keyTakeaways.title: Key Takeaways
items: Bow ties occur most commonly in oval, pear and marquise brilliant-style diamonds.
The pattern is caused by the interaction between the diamond’s facet arrangement, proportions, lighting and observer obstruction.
A bow tie is not an inclusion, colour concentration or surface damage.
A slight bow tie is not automatically a defect.
Contrast can help define a diamond’s pattern and apparent brightness.
Large, dark and persistent bow ties are generally less desirable.
A bow tie that brightens during movement is usually less concerning than one that remains dark.
The observer’s distance and position can change how strong the pattern appears.
A close-up photograph can exaggerate or hide a bow tie.
High-intensity spotlights can disguise inactive areas.
Table and depth percentages cannot independently predict bow-tie severity.
Length-to-width ratio describes the outline but does not provide a bow-tie grade.
Excellent polish and symmetry do not prove that the bow tie is minimal.
Standard GIA reports do not provide a separate bow-tie severity rating.
The setting cannot repair an unattractive facet pattern.
Compare similar diamonds under the same lighting and camera conditions.
The final decision should be based on darkness, width, balance, persistence and overall appearance.

whatIs.title: What Is the Diamond Bow Tie Effect?
introParagraphs: A bow tie is a central area of dark contrast that normally extends across the width of an elongated diamond.

GIA’s current technical definition describes the bow-tie effect as a darkened region in the centre of elongated shapes such as oval, pear and marquise diamonds. It occurs when light obscured by the observer is directed into the central viewing area by the diamond’s facet arrangement.

In simpler terms, a diamond’s facets act like small mirrors. They collect and return light from different directions. When the observer’s head and shoulders block part of that light, certain facets can reflect the darker obstruction back towards the observer.
The result is a bow-shaped pattern across the centre.
The pattern can appear:
closingParagraphs: The word “bow tie” describes an appearance. It is not an official clarity characteristic or colour grade.

whatCauses.title: What Causes a Bow Tie in a Diamond?
introParagraphs: The bow-tie effect comes from several interacting factors.

subsections.title: Elongated Shape
paragraphsBefore: Oval, pear and marquise diamonds distribute their brilliant-style facets across an elongated outline. This geometry creates different reflection patterns from those seen in a standard round brilliant.
GIA’s research into oval, pear and marquise diamond appearance found that elongation tends to produce bow ties across many proportion combinations and facet arrangements.

subsections.title: Facet Arrangement
paragraphsBefore: A diamond’s pavilion and crown facets determine how light travels through the stone and returns to the viewer.
Certain arrangements direct more observer-obscured light into the centre, producing a stronger dark pattern. Other arrangements distribute contrast more evenly across the diamond.

subsections.title: Pavilion Proportions
paragraphsBefore: Diamonds with unsuitable pavilion angles or depth relationships may show a more distracting bow tie.
A number printed on a report cannot independently predict the result because many facet angles and relationships influence the face-up pattern.

subsections.title: Observer Obstruction
paragraphsBefore: The viewer’s head, shoulders, camera and surrounding dark objects can block light.
This explains why a bow tie may appear stronger when:
bullets: The diamond is held close to the face
A camera lens is positioned very near the stone
The surrounding environment contains large dark areas
Light reaches the diamond from limited directions

isAlwaysBad.title: Is a Bow Tie Always Bad?
introParagraphs: No. A bow tie is not automatically bad.
Dark and bright facets work together to create contrast. Without contrast, a diamond can appear flat, washed out or visually undefined.
A mild bow tie may:
bullets: Brighten and darken attractively during movement
Blend with the diamond’s complete facet pattern
closingParagraphs: GIA’s marquise guidance explains that a slight bow tie can be visually appealing, while an excessively dark or wide pattern can become distracting.
The correct objective is therefore not necessarily to find a diamond with absolutely no dark contrast.
The objective is to avoid a bow tie that dominates the stone.

whenProblem.title: When Does a Bow Tie Become a Problem?
introParagraphs: A bow tie becomes problematic when its negative effect is stronger than its contribution to contrast.

subsections.title: Excessive Darkness
paragraphsBefore: A light or medium-grey pattern may integrate naturally with the rest of the diamond.
A nearly black central band can make the stone appear divided and may immediately attract attention away from its brightness.

subsections.title: Excessive Width
paragraphsBefore: A thin central pattern may be acceptable. A wide pattern that covers much of the diamond’s centre can reduce its lively face-up appearance.

subsections.title: Persistence
paragraphsBefore: Some bow ties brighten when the diamond moves. Others remain dark through several viewing angles.
GIA’s research distinguishes between bow ties that change during movement and those that remain persistent. Large, dark and persistent bow ties are generally considered a negative appearance factor.

subsections.title: Unevenness
paragraphsBefore: A bow tie should be assessed for balance.
One side should not appear:
paragraphsAfter: An uneven bow tie can make the complete facet pattern appear unbalanced.

subsections.title: Separation of the Diamond
paragraphsBefore: A severe bow tie can visually divide the diamond into two bright ends with a dead central band.
This is particularly noticeable when the centre remains dark while the tips or rounded ends flash brightly.

ovalBowTie.title: Oval Diamond Bow Tie Effect
introParagraphs: The oval diamond bow tie is generally visible across the stone’s middle, between its two rounded ends.
An attractive oval should show:
bullets: A bow tie that does not remain black
Balanced movement from left to right
No large dull areas beside the bow tie
closingParagraphs: GIA’s oval-cut diamond guide explains that observer obstruction creates the central contrast pattern and that the effect can become more noticeable when the face is closer to the diamond.

subsections.title: Oval Warning Signs
paragraphsBefore: Pause when:
bullets: The centre appears like a solid black band
The bow tie remains unchanged while the stone moves
One side is darker than the other
The ends sparkle but the centre remains inactive
The seller provides only a single face-up photograph
The video uses intense spotlighting without diffused light
paragraphsAfter: A more elongated oval may show a prominent bow tie, but ratio alone cannot predict severity. Two ovals with the same length-to-width ratio can display very different patterns.

pearBowTie.title: Pear-Shaped Diamond Bow Tie Effect
introParagraphs: The bow tie in a pear-shaped diamond normally crosses the belly between the rounded head and pointed end.
A well-performing pear should show:
bullets: A balanced transition from head to point
A bow tie that blends with movement
No large dark centre separating the head from the point
closingParagraphs: GIA’s pear-shaped diamond buying guidance notes that bow ties can range from light grey to black. The darker or larger the bow tie, the more it may detract from the face-up appearance.

subsections.title: Pear Warning Signs
paragraphsBefore: Look carefully when:
bullets: The rounded head is bright but the belly is dark
The bow tie stretches deeply into both wings
One wing becomes dark while the other remains bright
A strong bow tie is combined with a crooked outline
The pointed area also appears dull or grey
paragraphsAfter: The bow tie should be evaluated separately from durability. The pear’s point must also be checked for inclusions and protected by an appropriate setting.

marquiseBowTie.title: Marquise Diamond Bow Tie Effect
introParagraphs: Marquise diamonds commonly show a central bow tie between their two pointed ends.
Because the shape is strongly elongated, the bow tie can become an important part of its face-up appearance.
An attractive marquise should show:
closingParagraphs: GIA’s marquise diamond guide explains that the darker and wider the bow tie becomes, the more it can negatively affect appearance.

subsections.title: Marquise Warning Signs
paragraphsBefore: Pause when:
bullets: The centre forms a broad black band
Dark wings accompany the central bow tie
One point appears brighter than the other
The bow tie dominates the entire face-up view
The darkness remains unchanged during rotation
paragraphsAfter: Both marquise points must also be inspected for inclusions, extremely thin girdle areas and setting protection.

doesGiaReport.title: Does a GIA Report Show the Bow-Tie Effect?
introParagraphs: A standard GIA grading report does not provide a separate bow-tie grade or severity score.

As of 30 July 2026, GIA’s established overall cut-grading system remains restricted to standard round brilliant diamonds in the D-to-Z colour range. GIA is researching more advanced approaches for evaluating fancy-shaped diamond appearance.

Its June 2026 discussion, The Transformation of Diamond Cut Quality Grading, explains why fancy shapes require evaluation of movement, contrast, observer obstruction, patterning and personal visual preferences.
A report may still provide:
closingParagraphs: None of these fields independently tells the buyer how dark, wide or persistent the bow tie will appear.

closingParagraphs: Two diamonds can have similar report percentages while showing different contrast patterns.

doesRatioCause.title: Does Length-to-Width Ratio Cause a Bow Tie?
introParagraphs: Ratio can influence the diamond’s appearance, but it does not independently cause or grade the bow tie.

A longer outline may increase the opportunity for a strong central pattern, particularly when combined with unsuitable pavilion relationships. However, a strongly elongated diamond can still have an attractive and responsive centre.
Use ratio to choose the preferred outline.
Use visual inspection to judge the bow tie.

doPolishSymmetryPrevent.title: Do Excellent Polish and Symmetry Prevent a Bow Tie?
introParagraphs: No.
Polish evaluates the quality of the diamond’s finished facet surfaces. Symmetry evaluates the alignment, shape and placement of facets.
Excellent polish and symmetry are positive characteristics, but they do not guarantee:
closingParagraphs: A diamond can have Excellent polish and symmetry while still showing a distracting central bow tie.

canSettingHide.title: Can a Setting Hide or Repair a Bow Tie?
introParagraphs: A setting cannot correct the diamond’s internal facet pattern.
Prongs, halos and side stones may change the visual context around the centre diamond, but they do not repair a large, dark and persistent bow tie.

finalAnswer.title: Final Answer: Should You Buy a Diamond with a Bow Tie?
introParagraphs: Yes, a diamond with a slight bow tie can still be an excellent choice.
Do not reject a diamond merely because you can identify some central contrast. Instead, assess:
bullets: How dark the bow tie is
Whether it remains distracting at a normal distance
Whether the complete diamond remains lively
closingParagraphs: Avoid diamonds where the bow tie is large, black, uneven and persistent.
The best oval, pear or marquise diamond does not necessarily have zero contrast. It has a balanced pattern in which the bow tie supports the diamond’s appearance rather than dominating it.

items.question: What is the bow-tie effect in a diamond?
items.answer: The bow-tie effect is a dark contrast pattern that appears across the centre of certain elongated diamonds. It is most common in oval, pear and marquise brilliant-style diamonds.

items.question: What causes a diamond bow tie?
items.answer: It is caused by the interaction between the diamond’s elongated geometry, facet arrangement, proportions, surrounding light and observer obstruction. Some facets return the darker reflection created when the viewer blocks part of the available light.

items.question: Is a bow tie in a diamond always bad?
items.answer: No. A subtle and balanced bow tie can contribute useful contrast and visual depth. It becomes a concern when it is excessively dark, wide, uneven or persistent.

items.question: Which diamond shapes have the strongest bow-tie risk?
items.answer: Oval, pear and marquise diamonds are most commonly associated with the effect. Similar dark patterns can also appear in some heart, radiant and elongated cushion diamonds.

items.question: Does GIA grade the bow-tie effect?
items.answer: A standard GIA grading report does not provide a separate bow-tie grade or severity score. The diamond must be assessed visually under appropriate lighting and during movement.

items.question: How can I tell if a bow tie is too strong?
items.answer: A bow tie may be too strong when it appears black, covers a wide central area, divides the diamond visually and remains dark as the stone moves.

items.question: Can a diamond have no bow tie at all?
items.answer: Some diamonds show very little obvious central bow-tie contrast. However, the goal should be balanced light performance rather than the complete absence of dark reflections.

items.question: Can a setting hide a diamond bow tie?
items.answer: A setting may change the visual surroundings, but it cannot correct the diamond’s facet pattern. A large and persistent bow tie will generally remain visible after setting.

items.question: Can I judge a bow tie from an online video?
items.answer: A high-quality video can help when it shows slow movement, normal magnification, diffused lighting and ordinary room light. A single edited video under intense spotlights is insufficient.

items.question: Should I buy an oval diamond with a visible bow tie?
items.answer: You can buy it when the bow tie is subtle, balanced and responsive during movement. Avoid an oval with a broad black centre that remains distracting under several lighting conditions.

finalTakeaway.title: Judge the Bow Tie by Darkness, Width and Movement—Not by the Report Alone
introParagraphs: A slight bow tie can support contrast; a large, black and persistent pattern should stop a purchase.
Inspect elongated diamonds face-up, in motion and under realistic lighting before approving the stone.
